title: A new home saliva test to help diagnose adrenal insufficiency: finding out how well it works in the NHS
official: Evaluating the implementation and uptake of waking saliva cortisone: a new home-based test for adrenal insufficiency
summary:
Background and study aims
Adrenal insufficiency is a condition where the body does not produce enough of a hormone called cortisol. Cortisol is important for helping the body cope with illness, injury and stress. People with adrenal insufficiency can experience symptoms such as tiredness, dizziness, feeling sick and muscle aches. If the condition is not diagnosed and treated, it can lead to a serious, potentially life-threatening illness called an adrenal crisis.
Currently, people who may have adrenal insufficiency usually need blood tests or a hospital-based test called a short synacthen test. This test involves having an injection and several blood tests over an approximately 2-hour period. It can also involve long waiting times and travelling to hospital.
A new test called a waking salivary cortisone (WSC) test offers another way of testing for adrenal insufficiency. It involves collecting a saliva sample at home shortly after waking up. The sample is then sent to a laboratory to measure cortisone levels (the equivalent of cortisol in saliva).
Previous research suggests that this test can help identify people who are unlikely or likely to have adrenal insufficiency, potentially reducing the need for hospital-based testing.
This study aims to find out how well this home saliva test can be introduced and used across different NHS hospitals. The study will:
1. Find out how often healthcare professionals use the saliva test instead of existing tests
2. Understand what helps or makes it difficult for NHS hospitals to introduce the new test
3. Find out what patients and parents think about using the test at home
4. Explore whether the new test could save time and money for patients and the NHS
5. Develop guidance to help other NHS hospitals introduce the test in the future

Who can participate?
Patients having adrenal insufficiency testing as part of their usual NHS care will be included in the evaluation of how the new test is introduced and used. Patients do not need to give individual consent for their routine healthcare information to be included in this part of the study. However, people who have registered with the NHS England National Data Opt-Out will not have their information included.

What does the study involve?
The study will introduce the home saliva test into four NHS hospitals and look at how it is used in everyday healthcare. The study will involve three main stages:
1. Before introducing the test: Collecting information about how people are currently tested for adrenal insufficiency.
2. Introducing the test: Supporting the four NHS hospitals to start using the home saliva test and providing training for healthcare professionals and laboratory staff.
3. After introducing the test: Collecting information for a further 12 months to see how the new test is being used and whether it has improved testing services.
At each of these stages, the research team will collect information on a monthly basis from the four hospitals. They will look at:
1. How many people have the saliva test compared with existing blood and hospital tests
2. How many samples are successfully collected and returned
3. How long people wait for their test and results
4. How many people need further hospital-based testing
5. Whether introducing the saliva test changes the costs of testing
This study is not a trial in which patients are randomly allocated to different tests. Healthcare professionals will continue to decide which tests are appropriate for each patient.
Around 320 adults and 80 parents or legal guardians of children who are offered the saliva test will be invited to complete a short questionnaire. The questionnaire will ask about their views on the test, including how easy it was to use and whether they found it acceptable. People can complete the questionnaire online, by post or, where needed, with help over the telephone.
Healthcare professionals and laboratory staff involved in introducing the test will be invited to take part in interviews. The interviews will explore what worked well, any difficulties they experienced and what could be improved when introducing the test into NHS services.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The study may help improve the way people are tested for adrenal insufficiency in the future. The home saliva test could:
1. Reduce the number of hospital visits needed for testing
2. Avoid the need for needles and injections for some people
3. Make testing more convenient for adults and children
4. Reduce waiting times for diagnosis
5. Help the NHS save time and money
There may not be a direct benefit to people whose information or questionnaire responses are included in the study.
The saliva test will be introduced as part of usual NHS care. Patients will not be recruited as research participants and decisions about which tests patients need will remain with their healthcare professionals.
The study will use confidential patient information. Steps will be taken to protect this information, including removing personal details before information is shared with the wider research team. Patients will also have the option for their data not to be collected for the purposes of this research using the National Data Opt-Out service.

Where is the study run from?
The study is led by researchers at the University of Sheffield, Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, the University of Hull and Manchester University Hospital NHS Foundation Trust (UK), working in partnership with the four participating NHS Trusts:
1. King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
2. Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
3. Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust
4. University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust
Hull Health Trials Unit at the University of Hull will support the management of the study.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2027 to June 2029

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
1. Dr Charlotte Elder, c.j.elder@sheffield.ac.uk
2. Prof. Miguel Debono, miguel.debono@nhs.net
